\chapter{Which One in the Line}
\label{ch:mr-ordinals}
\hlchaptermodality{60}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say first to fifth in Marathi, tell the four ordinals Marathi inherited whole from the ones it builds, and agree any of them with a masculine, feminine or neuter thing.}

Complete MR-R60-first-to-fifth and run pahilaa to paachvaa, then say which one of the five you could have worked out.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[dusrā]{\mr{दुसरा} (dusrā) — the second, and the set it belongs to}

\label{lesson:MR-C60-dusra-ordinal}



\begin{quote}
A second kind of number word starts here, so the recalls come first, at the four growing distances this book measures.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{rupayā} — \textbf{R1}, one chapter back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{vīs} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{sahā} — \textbf{R3}, twenty-four lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{kitī?} — \textbf{R4}, ninety-one lessons back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: you already own one of these}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{दुसरा}} — \emph{dusrā} — \textbf{the second, the other}
\end{quote}

Chapter thirty-one gave you this word as the partner \textbf{\mr{एक}} needed: \textbf{\mr{एक} \mr{चहा} \mr{आणि} \mr{दुसरा} \mr{पाणी}}. Its gloss said \emph{the other, \textbf{the second}}, and its etymology said it is \textbf{\mr{दोन}} wearing an ending.

Nothing about it changes today. What changes is that it stops being one word and becomes a member of a set.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: two sets of number words, not one}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{the question} & \textbf{the set} & \textbf{example} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\mr{किती}?} — how many? & \textbf{\mr{एक}, \mr{दोन}, \mr{तीन}, \mr{चार}, \mr{पाच}} & \textbf{\mr{दोन} \mr{चहा}} — two teas \\
\emph{which one in the line?} & \textbf{\mr{दुसरा}} and its fellows & \textbf{\mr{दुसरा} \mr{चहा}} — the second tea \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{\mr{दोन} \mr{चहा}} and \textbf{\mr{दुसरा} \mr{चहा}} are not the same order at a stall: the first asks for two cups, the second picks one cup out of a line.

This chapter teaches the second set, and \textbf{it teaches no new word today} — because the set already has a member in your mouth, and noticing that is the honest first step.

An ordinal is an ordinary adjective in \textbf{-\mr{आ}}, so it takes the three endings chapter forty-nine taught on \textbf{\mr{मोठा}}: \textbf{\mr{दुसरा}}, \textbf{\mr{दुसरी}}, \textbf{\mr{दुसरं}}. Every word in this chapter and the next behaves this way, and it will not be repeated for each one.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{don chahā}, then \emph{dusrā chahā}
  \item the three agreeing forms — \emph{dusrā}, \emph{dusrī}, \emph{dusraṁ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many sets of number words does Marathi keep? (\textbf{Two.}) How many new words did this lesson teach? (\textbf{None.})

Sources: \href{https://dsal.uchicago.edu/cgi-bin/app/molesworth\_query.py?qs=\%E0\%A4\%A6\%E0\%A5\%81\%E0\%A4\%B8\%E0\%A4\%B0\%E0\%A4\%BE\&searchhws=yes}{Molesworth, \emph{A Dictionary, Marathi and English}, p. 420 (DSAL)}; \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%A6\%E0\%A5\%81\%E0\%A4\%B8\%E0\%A4\%B0\%E0\%A4\%BE}{Wiktionary: \mr{दुसरा}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tisrā]{\mr{तिसरा} (tisrā) — third}

\label{lesson:MR-C60-tisra}



\begin{quote}
Four recalls, at four distances.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say how many sets of number words Marathi keeps — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} write the \emph{ai} sign on \textbf{\mr{क}} — \textbf{R2}, five lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{dahā} — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ghar} — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{तिसरा}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{तिसरा}} — \emph{tisrā} — \textbf{third}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{तिसरं} \mr{घर}} — \emph{tisraṁ ghar} — \textbf{the third house}
\end{quote}

Put the two words you now have side by side against the numbers under them:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{how many} & \textbf{which one in the line} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\mr{दोन}} (\emph{don}) & \textbf{\mr{दुसरा}} (\emph{dusrā}) \\
\textbf{\mr{तीन}} (\emph{tīn}) & \textbf{\mr{तिसरा}} (\emph{tisrā}) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The number is still visible in both. \textbf{\mr{दोन}} leaves \textbf{\mr{दु}-}, \textbf{\mr{तीन}} leaves \textbf{\mr{ति}-}, and the same \textbf{-\mr{सरा}} sits on the end of each.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: two is not yet a rule}]
It would be pleasant to say \textbf{-\mr{सरा}} is how Marathi makes ordinals. It is not, and this book will not claim it: \textbf{-\mr{सरा}} appears on these two words and on no others in the language. What the pair does prove is smaller and true — that the which-one set is \emph{related} to the how-many set, close enough for the eye to catch it.

Keep the vowel change in view too. \emph{don} has an \textbf{o} and \emph{dusrā} has a \textbf{u}; \emph{tīn} has a long \textbf{ī} and \emph{tisrā} a short \textbf{i}. The number is visible, not untouched.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{dusrā}, then \emph{tisrā}
  \item the number inside each — \emph{don}, \emph{tīn}
  \item \emph{tisraṁ ghar} — the third house
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which number is inside \textbf{\mr{तिसरा}}? (\textbf{\mr{तीन}}.) Is \textbf{-\mr{सरा}} a rule you can use on any number? (\textbf{No} — it is on these two words only.)

Sources: \href{https://dsal.uchicago.edu/cgi-bin/app/molesworth\_query.py?qs=\%E0\%A4\%A4\%E0\%A4\%BF\%E0\%A4\%B8\%E0\%A4\%B0\%E0\%A4\%BE\&searchhws=yes}{Molesworth, \emph{A Dictionary, Marathi and English}, p. 381 (DSAL)}; \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/marathi.htm}{Omniglot: Numbers in Marathi}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pahilā]{\mr{पहिला} (pahilā) — first}

\label{lesson:MR-C60-pahila}



\begin{quote}
Four recalls, at four distances.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{tisrā} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{paise} — \textbf{R2}, five lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{akrā} — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{khoolī} — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{पहिला}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{पहिला}} — \emph{pahilā} — \textbf{first}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{पहिली} \mr{खोली}} — \emph{pahilī khoolī} — \textbf{the first room}
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: why \emph{first} arrives third}]
Go looking for the number inside this one:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{how many} & \textbf{which one in the line} & \textbf{the number, still visible?} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\mr{दोन}} & \textbf{\mr{दुसरा}} & yes — \textbf{\mr{दु}-} \\
\textbf{\mr{तीन}} & \textbf{\mr{तिसरा}} & yes — \textbf{\mr{ति}-} \\
\textbf{\mr{एक}} & \textbf{\mr{पहिला}} & \textbf{no} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

There is no \textbf{\mr{एक}} anywhere in \textbf{\mr{पहिला}}. Not a letter of it.

That is why the chapter did not begin here. A word can only be seen to break a shape once the shape has been seen holding, and you have now watched the number stay visible in two words running. The third case is a surprise.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: what this book claims about \mr{पहिला}, and what it does not}]
Molesworth's dictionary gives \textbf{\mr{पहिला}} twice over — as an adjective, \textquotedblleft{}the first\textquotedblright{}, and, declined, as an adverb, \textquotedblleft{}at first; in the beginning\textquotedblright{}. Marathi never built a separate word for putting an \emph{action} first; it re-used this one.

\textbf{This lesson teaches the adjective only} — a thing picked out of a line, as in \textbf{\mr{पहिली} \mr{खोली}}. The adverb is named so you recognise it, and not drilled. The words that order a sequence — \emph{before}, \emph{after}, \emph{next} — are not taught here.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{pahilā}, \emph{dusrā}, \emph{tisrā}
  \item which of the three has no number inside it — \emph{\textbf{pahilā}}
  \item \emph{pahilī khoolī} — the first room
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which number is inside \textbf{\mr{पहिला}}? (\textbf{None} — \textbf{\mr{एक}} is not in it.) Why was this word not the first one in the chapter? (\textbf{Nothing had been seen for it to break yet.})

Sources: \href{https://dsal.uchicago.edu/cgi-bin/app/molesworth\_query.py?qs=\%E0\%A4\%AA\%E0\%A4\%B9\%E0\%A4\%BF\%E0\%A4\%B2\%E0\%A4\%BE\&searchhws=yes}{Molesworth, \emph{A Dictionary, Marathi and English}, p. 497 (DSAL)}; \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/marathi.htm}{Omniglot: Numbers in Marathi}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[chauthā]{\mr{चौथा} (chauthā) — fourth}

\label{lesson:MR-C60-chautha}



\begin{quote}
Four recalls, at four distances.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{pahilā} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{rupayā} — \textbf{R2}, five lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{bārā} — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{gharāt} and name what the \textbf{-\mr{आ}} did to \textbf{\mr{घर}} — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{चौथा}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{चौथा}} — \emph{chauthā} — \textbf{fourth}
\end{quote}

The \emph{au} sign you wrote in chapter fifty-six is the visible part of this word. \textbf{\mr{चार}} (\emph{chār}) gives \textbf{\mr{चौ}-} (\emph{chau-}), and then an ending you have not seen before takes over: \textbf{-\mr{था}}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: four words, three shapes, no rule}]
The chapter's four words, laid out against their numbers:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{how many} & \textbf{which one in the line} & \textbf{what happened} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\mr{एक}} & \textbf{\mr{पहिला}} & nothing survives \\
\textbf{\mr{दोन}} & \textbf{\mr{दुसरा}} & \textbf{-\mr{सरा}} \\
\textbf{\mr{तीन}} & \textbf{\mr{तिसरा}} & \textbf{-\mr{सरा}} \\
\textbf{\mr{चार}} & \textbf{\mr{चौथा}} & \textbf{-\mr{था}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Three different shapes across four words. Marathi did not build these; it \textbf{inherited} them, each one worn down separately over centuries — Molesworth records \textbf{\mr{चौथा}} as coming straight from Sanskrit \textbf{\mr{चतुर्थ}}.

So do not look for a rule here. \textbf{There is none, and this book will not invent one}: these four are four words, and the honest instruction is to learn them as four words. What matters is that the list ENDS. There are exactly four of them, and you now have all four.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{pahilā dusrā tisrā chauthā} — the four, in order
  \item which two share an ending — \emph{\textbf{dusrā}} and \emph{\textbf{tisrā}}
  \item \emph{chauthā rupayā} — the fourth rupee
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many of these four can you predict from the number? (\textbf{None} — they are inherited, not built.) How many are there in all? (\textbf{Four.})

Sources: \href{https://dsal.uchicago.edu/cgi-bin/app/molesworth\_query.py?qs=\%E0\%A4\%9A\%E0\%A5\%8C\%E0\%A4\%A5\%E0\%A4\%BE\&searchhws=yes}{Molesworth, \emph{A Dictionary, Marathi and English}, p. 296 (DSAL)}; \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/marathi.htm}{Omniglot: Numbers in Marathi}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pāchvā]{\mr{पाचवा} (pāchvā) — fifth, and the seam}

\label{lesson:MR-C60-pachva}



\begin{quote}
Four recalls, at four distances.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{chauthā} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ekoṇīs} and take it apart — \textbf{R2}, ten lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} write the \emph{au} sign — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ghar} — \textbf{R4}, eighty-three lessons back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{पाचवा}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{पाचवा}} — \emph{pāchvā} — \textbf{fifth}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{पाचवं} \mr{घर}} — \emph{pāchvaṁ ghar} — \textbf{the fifth house}
\end{quote}

Say \textbf{\mr{पाच}} and then say \textbf{\mr{पाचवा}}. The number did not change at all. Nothing was worn down, nothing was replaced: \textbf{\mr{पाच}} is still sitting there whole, with \textbf{-\mr{वा}} added behind it.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: -\mr{वा}, and where the language changes its mind}]
Here is the whole chapter in one column, with the break marked:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{how many} & \textbf{which one in the line} \\
\midrule
 & \textbf{\mr{एक}} & \textbf{\mr{पहिला}} \\
 & \textbf{\mr{दोन}} & \textbf{\mr{दुसरा}} \\
 & \textbf{\mr{तीन}} & \textbf{\mr{तिसरा}} \\
 & \textbf{\mr{चार}} & \textbf{\mr{चौथा}} \\
\textbf{— the seam —} &  &  \\
 & \textbf{\mr{पाच}} & \textbf{\mr{पाच}} + \textbf{\mr{वा}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Above the line, four words Marathi received from its ancestors, each worn down its own way, none predictable from the number.

Below the line, a \textbf{rule}: take the number and put \textbf{-\mr{वा}} on it. That is all there is, and it does not stop at five. Six, seven, ten, twenty, a hundred — the next chapter walks the rest of the way, and every one of them is made this way.

You have therefore learned two different kinds of thing in one chapter. Four words, which had to be memorised. And one ending, which does not.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{pāch}, then \emph{pāchvā}
  \item \emph{pāchvaṁ ghar} — the fifth house
  \item the four that had to be memorised — \emph{pahilā dusrā tisrā chauthā}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What do you add to a number to make an ordinal? (\textbf{-\mr{वा}}.) At which number does that start working? (\textbf{Five} — everything before it is a word, not a rule.)

Sources: \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/marathi.htm}{Omniglot: Numbers in Marathi}; \href{https://dsal.uchicago.edu/cgi-bin/app/molesworth\_query.py?qs=\%E0\%A4\%AA\%E0\%A4\%BE\%E0\%A4\%9A\%E0\%A4\%B5\%E0\%A4\%BE\&searchhws=yes}{Molesworth, \emph{A Dictionary, Marathi and English}, p. 500 (DSAL)}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pahilā · dusrā · tisrā · chauthā …]{First to fifth, and where the language changed its mind}

\label{lesson:MR-R60-first-to-fifth}



\begin{quote}
Four recalls, at four distances, before the run.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{pāchvā} and the ending that made it — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say how many sets of number words Marathi keeps — \textbf{R2}, five lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the three agreeing endings of \textbf{\mr{मोठा}} — \textbf{R3}, fifty-three lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{madhye} — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{pahilā dusrā tisrā chauthā pāchvā} — the run, without stopping
  \item the four that had to be memorised, and the one that did not
  \item \emph{pāchvaṁ}, \emph{pāchvī}, \emph{pāchvā} — the three agreeing endings on the fifth
\end{itemize}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built this chapter, in one number}]
Of the five ordinals in this chapter, \textbf{one} was built and \textbf{four} were memorised. That is the worst ratio you will ever see in this set, and it is worth saying out loud, because the next chapter reverses it completely: five more ordinals, and every single one of them built.

The break sits between \textbf{\mr{चौथा}} and \textbf{\mr{पाचवा}}. Everything before it is a word Marathi received. Everything after it is a word Marathi makes.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Between which two ordinals does the seam fall? (\textbf{\mr{चौथा}} and \textbf{\mr{पाचवा}}.) What sits on the far side of it? (\textbf{A rule — the number, plus -\mr{वा}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
